library(tidyverse)
library(p8105.datasets)
library(patchwork)
library(knitr)

# Problem 1 — NY NOAA
## Import and describe the dataset
```{r}
data("ny_noaa")

dim(ny_noaa)

ny_noaa |>
  summarize(
    across(
      c(prcp, snow, snwd, tmax, tmin),
      ~ mean(is.na(.x)) * 100
    )
  ) |>
  kable(digits = 1)
```
### Dataset description
The NY NOAA dataset contains `r nrow(ny_noaa)` observations and `r ncol(ny_noaa)` variables from `r n_distinct(ny_noaa$id)` weather stations in New York State. Each row represents a weather observation at a specific station on a particular date. The dataset includes station ID, date, precipitation (`prcp`), snowfall (`snow`), snow depth (`snwd`), maximum temperature (`tmax`), and minimum temperature (`tmin`).

Missing data are an important issue. Approximately `r round(100 * mean(is.na(ny_noaa$tmax)), 1)`% of maximum temperature observations and `r round(100 * mean(is.na(ny_noaa$tmin)), 1)`% of minimum temperature observations are missing. The missing percentages are `r round(100 * mean(is.na(ny_noaa$prcp)), 1)`% for precipitation, `r round(100 * mean(is.na(ny_noaa$snow)), 1)`% for snowfall, and `r round(100 * mean(is.na(ny_noaa$snwd)), 1)`% for snow depth. This may affect comparisons across stations and years.

## Data cleaning

```{r}
noaa_df =
  ny_noaa |>
  mutate(
    year = lubridate::year(date),
    month = lubridate::month(date),
    day = lubridate::day(date),
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10,
    prcp = prcp / 10
  )
```

### Most commonly observed snowfall values

```{r}
noaa_df |>
  count(snow, sort = TRUE) |>
  drop_na(snow) |>
  slice_head(n = 10) |>
  kable()
```

### Discussion

I extracted year, month, and day from the date variable. Maximum and minimum temperatures were converted from tenths of degrees Celsius to degrees Celsius, and precipitation was converted from tenths of millimeters to millimeters. Snowfall and snow depth were already recorded in millimeters.

The most commonly observed snowfall value is 0 mm, with `r sum(noaa_df$snow == 0, na.rm = TRUE)` observations. This is expected because most days have no measurable snowfall. Other common nonzero values include 25 mm, 13 mm, and 51 mm. These values are approximately equivalent to one inch, half an inch, and two inches, suggesting that some snowfall measurements were recorded in inch-based increments and then converted to millimeters.

## Average maximum temperature in January and July

```{r}
noaa_jan_jul =
  noaa_df |>
  filter(month %in% c(1, 7)) |>
  mutate(
    month_label = factor(
      if_else(month == 1, "January", "July"),
      levels = c("January", "July")
    )
  ) |>
  group_by(id, year, month_label) |>
  summarize(
    mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  drop_na(mean_tmax)
```
```{r, fig.width=9, fig.asp=.6, out.width="90%"}
noaa_jan_jul |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, color = month_label, group = id)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .3, size = .5) +
  geom_line(alpha = .15) +
  facet_grid(. ~ month_label) +
  viridis::scale_color_viridis(discrete = TRUE) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Maximum Temperature in January and July",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Average Maximum Temperature (°C)"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

### Discussion

The two panels show a clear seasonal difference, with average maximum temperatures generally much higher in July than in January. Temperatures vary across stations and years, reflecting differences in location and weather conditions.

There are some unusually high or low station-year averages. These may reflect unusual weather conditions, differences between stations, or incomplete observations. In particular, averages calculated from only a small number of available days should be interpreted cautiously.

## Maximum and minimum temperature and snowfall distribution

```{r, fig.width=11, fig.asp=.5, out.width="100%"}
ggp_temp =
  noaa_df |>
  drop_na(tmax, tmin) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tmax, y = tmin)) +
  geom_bin2d(bins = 30) +
  viridis::scale_fill_viridis() +
  labs(
    title = "Maximum vs Minimum Temperature",
    x = "Maximum Temperature (°C)",
    y = "Minimum Temperature (°C)",
    fill = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_bw()

ggp_snow =
  noaa_df |>
  filter(snow > 0, snow < 100) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = snow, group = year)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(1985, 2010, 5)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Snowfall Distribution by Year",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Snowfall (mm)"
  ) +
  theme_bw()

ggp_temp + ggp_snow
```
### Discussion
Maximum and minimum temperatures show a strong positive relationship. Days with higher maximum temperatures generally also have higher minimum temperatures. Most observations are concentrated in the middle of the temperature range, while extreme values are less common.
For snowfall between 0 and 100 mm, the distributions vary across years. However, the overall ranges are relatively similar, and there is no clear increasing or decreasing trend over time.

# Problem 2

## Import and clean demographic data

```{r}
nhanes_demo =
  read_csv(
    "./data/nhanes_covar.csv",
    skip = 4
  ) |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  filter(age >= 21) |>
  drop_na(sex, age, bmi, education) |>
  mutate(
    sex = factor(
      sex,
      levels = c(1, 2),
      labels = c("Male", "Female")
    ),
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3),
      labels = c(
        "Less than high school",
        "High school equivalent",
        "More than high school"
      )
    )
  )
```

## Import and tidy accelerometer data

```{r}
nhanes_accel =
  read_csv("./data/nhanes_accel.csv") |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  pivot_longer(
    min1:min1440,
    names_to = "minute",
    names_prefix = "min",
    values_to = "mims"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    minute = as.numeric(minute) - 1
  )
```

## Merge the datasets

```{r}
nhanes_df =
  nhanes_demo |>
  inner_join(
    nhanes_accel,
    by = "seqn"
  )

nhanes_df |>
  summarize(
    participants = n_distinct(seqn),
    observations = n()
  )
```

### Data cleaning discussion

The demographic dataset was imported by skipping the first four non-data rows. I excluded participants younger than 21 and participants with missing demographic information. Sex was recoded as Male or Female, and education was converted into three labeled categories.

The accelerometer dataset contains minute-level MIMS measurements over a 24-hour period. I used `pivot_longer()` to convert the data from wide to long format and created a numeric variable representing minutes since midnight. Finally, I combined the two datasets using `inner_join()` by participant ID (`seqn`) to retain participants appearing in both datasets.

## Number of men and women by education

```{r}
nhanes_demo |>
  count(
    education,
    sex,
    name = "n_participants"
  ) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = sex,
    values_from = n_participants,
    values_fill = 0
  ) |>
  kable(
    caption = "Number of Participants by Education and Sex"
  )
```

### Discussion

The cleaned demographic dataset contains `r nrow(nhanes_demo)` participants. The largest education group is More than high school, followed by High school equivalent and Less than high school.

Men and women have similar counts in the Less than high school and More than high school groups. However, the High school equivalent category contains more men than women.

## Age distributions by sex and education

```{r, fig.width=9, fig.asp=.6, out.width="90%"}
nhanes_demo |>
  ggplot(aes(x = sex, y = age, fill = sex)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = .6) +
  facet_wrap(~education, nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Age Distribution by Sex and Education",
    x = "Sex",
    y = "Age (Years)",
    fill = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

### Discussion

The age distributions differ across education categories. Participants in the Less than high school group tend to be older, whereas those in the More than high school group tend to be younger.

Within the High school equivalent category, female participants are generally older than male participants. The distributions of men and women overlap considerably in the other education groups.

## Total daily activity versus age

```{r}
nhanes_total =
  nhanes_df |>
  group_by(seqn, age, sex, bmi, education) |>
  summarize(
    total_mims = sum(mims, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

```{r, fig.width=9, fig.asp=.6, out.width="90%"}
nhanes_total |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = total_mims, color = sex)) +
  geom_point(alpha = .6) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~education, nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Total Daily Activity by Age, Sex, and Education",
    x = "Age (Years)",
    y = "Total Daily MIMS",
    color = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```
### Discussion

Overall, total daily activity tends to decrease with age, particularly among older participants. The relationship between age and activity varies across education groups, and the smoothed curves suggest some differences between males and females. However, these sex-related differences are not consistent across all education levels.

There is also considerable variation in activity levels among individuals of similar ages. Although the patterns differ across education groups, the distributions overlap substantially. These findings suggest associations between age, sex, education, and physical activity, but they do not establish causality.

## 24-hour activity patterns

```{r, fig.width=10, fig.asp=.5, out.width="100%"}
nhanes_time =
  nhanes_df |>
  group_by(education, sex, minute) |>
  summarize(
    mean_mims = mean(mims, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

nhanes_time |>
  ggplot(aes(x = minute, y = mean_mims, color = sex)) +
  geom_line(alpha = .4) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_grid(. ~ education) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = c(0, 360, 720, 1080),
    labels = c("12 AM", "6 AM", "12 PM", "6 PM")
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "24-Hour Activity Patterns by Sex and Education",
    x = "Time of Day",
    y = "Mean MIMS",
    color = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```
### Discussion
Activity levels are generally lowest during the early morning hours and increase after approximately 6 AM. Activity remains relatively high during the daytime before decreasing in the evening.
The three education groups show similar overall daily patterns, although the activity levels and shapes of the curves differ somewhat. Differences between males and females are also visible, particularly during the daytime, but these differences are not consistent across all education groups.

# Problem 3

## Import and clean Citi Bike data

```{r}
citibike_df =
  bind_rows(
    read_csv("./data/Jan 2020 Citi.csv") |>
      mutate(year = 2020, month = "January"),

    read_csv("./data/July 2020 Citi.csv") |>
      mutate(year = 2020, month = "July"),

    read_csv("./data/Jan 2024 Citi.csv") |>
      mutate(year = 2024, month = "January"),

    read_csv("./data/July 2024 Citi.csv") |>
      mutate(year = 2024, month = "July")
  ) |>
  mutate(
    month = factor(
      month,
      levels = c("January", "July")
    ),
    weekdays = factor(
      weekdays,
      levels = c(
        "Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday",
        "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday"
      )
    ),
    member_casual = factor(
      member_casual,
      levels = c("casual", "member")
    ),
    rideable_type = factor(
      rideable_type,
      levels = c("classic_bike", "electric_bike")
    )
  )
```

## Describe the dataset

```{r}
citibike_df |>
  summarize(
    n_rides = n(),
    n_unique_rides = n_distinct(ride_id),
    n_missing_start_station = sum(is.na(start_station_name))
  )
```

### Discussion

The combined Citi Bike dataset contains `r nrow(citibike_df)` observations and `r ncol(citibike_df)` variables, representing a 1% sample of rides lasting less than four hours taken in January and July of 2020 and 2024.

Key variables include ride ID, bike type, day of the week, ride duration, starting and ending stations, and membership status. During data cleaning, I imported the four CSV files, created year and month variables, combined the datasets using `bind_rows()`, and converted categorical variables into factors with meaningful levels.

The dataset includes both classic and electric bikes, as well as casual riders and Citi Bike members. Some station names are missing, but these observations were retained because they still contain useful information for other analyses.

## Number of rides by year, month, and membership

```{r}
citibike_df |>
  count(
    year,
    month,
    member_casual,
    name = "n_rides"
  ) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = member_casual,
    values_from = n_rides,
    values_fill = 0
  ) |>
  kable(
    caption = "Number of Rides by Year, Month, and Membership"
  )
```
### Discussion

Members account for the majority of rides in all four months. The number of rides is higher in July than in January for both years and both membership categories.

The July 2024 sample contains substantially more rides than the July 2020 sample. Casual ridership also appears to increase considerably between 2020 and 2024.

These counts are based on the provided 1% samples rather than the full Citi Bike system.

## Five most popular starting stations in July 2024

```{r}
citibike_df |>
  filter(
    year == 2024,
    month == "July",
    !is.na(start_station_name)
  ) |>
  count(
    start_station_name,
    name = "n_rides",
    sort = TRUE
  ) |>
  slice_head(n = 5) |>
  kable(
    caption = "Top Five Starting Stations in July 2024"
  )
```

### Discussion

Pier 61 at Chelsea Piers was the most popular starting station in July 2024, with 163 rides in the sample. The other leading stations were University Pl & E 14 St, W 21 St & 6 Ave, West St & Chambers St, and W 31 St & 7 Ave.

These results indicate that several busy Manhattan locations accounted for a relatively large number of sampled rides.

## Median ride duration by weekday, month, and year

```{r, fig.width=9, fig.asp=.6, out.width="90%"}
citibike_median =
  citibike_df |>
  group_by(year, month, weekdays) |>
  summarize(
    median_duration = median(duration, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

citibike_median |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = weekdays,
      y = median_duration,
      color = month,
      group = month
    )
  ) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_line(linewidth = .8) +
  facet_wrap(~year, nrow = 1) +
  labs(
    title = "Median Ride Duration by Weekday, Month, and Year",
    x = "Day of the Week",
    y = "Median Ride Duration (Minutes)",
    color = "Month"
  ) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  )
```

### Discussion

Median ride durations are generally longer in July than in January in both years. This may reflect greater recreational riding during warmer months.

Weekend rides tend to be longer than weekday rides, especially in July 2020. In July 2020, the median ride duration was approximately 16.5 minutes on both Saturday and Sunday, compared with about 13–14 minutes on most weekdays.

Median ride durations in 2024 are generally shorter than those in 2020. For example, July 2024 median durations are approximately 9–11 minutes across the week, compared with approximately 13–17 minutes in July 2020.

These patterns suggest variation by season, weekday, and year, although the descriptive analysis does not establish the causes of these differences.

## Ride duration distributions in 2024

```{r, fig.width=9, fig.asp=.6, out.width="90%"}
citibike_df |>
  filter(year == 2024) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = rideable_type,
      y = duration,
      fill = member_casual
    )
  ) +
  geom_boxplot(
    alpha = .7,
    outlier.shape = NA
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~month, nrow = 1) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 60)) +
  labs(
    title = "Ride Duration by Bike Type and Membership in 2024",
    x = "Bike Type",
    y = "Ride Duration (Minutes)",
    fill = "Membership",
    caption = "The displayed y-axis is limited to 0–60 minutes"
  )+
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

## Median ride duration table

```{r}
citibike_df |>
  filter(year == 2024) |>
  group_by(
    month,
    member_casual,
    rideable_type
  ) |>
  summarize(
    n_rides = n(),
    median_duration = median(duration, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  kable(
    digits = 1,
    caption = "Ride Duration by Month, Membership, and Bike Type"
  )
```

### Discussion

Casual riders generally have longer ride durations than Citi Bike members in both January and July 2024. Ride durations also tend to be longer in July than in January.

Among casual riders, classic bike rides have longer median durations than electric bike rides in both months. In January, the median duration is approximately 12.7 minutes for classic bikes and 9.3 minutes for electric bikes. In July, the corresponding medians are approximately 15.6 and 12.9 minutes.

Among members, the difference between bike types is smaller. In January, the median durations are approximately 7.3 minutes for classic bikes and 7.6 minutes for electric bikes. In July, they increase to approximately 7.7 and 9.2 minutes, respectively.

Overall, membership status and month appear to be strongly associated with ride duration, while the relationship with bike type differs between casual riders and members.
